newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Globalisation raises challenges for Asian markets.
newsitem.headline: Globalisation raises challenges for Asian markets.

text.p: Financial policy-makers gathered on Friday to debate the benefits of Asian market interdependence as integration into the global economy puts ever greater strains on the region's fledgling regulatory frameworks.

"Increasing trade and financial sector integration -- in the global economy and in the region -- offers enormous potential benefits but will also pose new challenges for Asian countries," Michel Camdessus, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, told the conference in Hong Kong.
Asia's share of world trade has ballooned over the last decade and capital flows to the region have soared, contributing to strong growth and the rapid development of financial markets.

But while increased participation in global markets brings benefits, it also brings problems that must be addressed, Camdessus told an IMF-Hong Kong Monetary Authority Conference on financial integration in Asia and the role of Hong Kong.
As Asian countries increase trade and financial links with the rest of the world and with each other, they become vulnerable to financial crises in other countries.
"Accordingly, individual economies will have an increasing interest in the economic prosperity and stability of others," the IMF chief said.
Anwar Ibrahim, Malaysia's deputy prime minister and minister of finance, said the risks that accompany greater financial integration and increasing openness were obvious.
"They include instability, increased risk-taking by financial institutions and pressures on international payment and settlement systems," he said.

Delegates to the conference, taking place in the world's most open market, stressed that each country must maintain prudent fiscal policy, a proper regulatory framework and strong banking systems to guard against instability.
Asian countries also must act together to avert crises that could wreak havoc on the region's currency and financial markets, they said.
Many of the countries in the region already have signed bilateral repurchase agreements (repos) to provide liquidity if one or more Asian currency is attacked.
But so far, there have been few other formal pacts among Asian countries to protect against systemic financial shocks, and Friday's meeting did not offer any new initiatives.

Joseph Yam, chief executive of the HKMA, has for some time been a vocal proponent of an Asia-wide payments system to assure real-time settlement across borders, but response to the suggestion has been mixed.

Likewise, while some Asian policy-makers have been keen to create a regional banking supervisory body along the lines of the Basle-based Bank for International Settlements, others have been decidedly lukewarm on the idea.
Asian leaders do agree, however, on the need for better communication between countries.

China and Hong Kong have signed a repo agreement in case of a currency crisis, but Chen Yuan, deputy governor at the People's Bank of China, said cooperation between the two monetary authorities was otherwise informal.

"We don't have any specific instrument to use between us other than the repo agreement, but we already keep very close contact," he said, adding "that is the most efficient way to cooperate on market disturbances".

Malaysia's Anwar said that rather than create new agencies to facilitate cooperation, Asian countries should operate within established regional groups, such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
